add/gate: Zoom in on one node of a graph: an add gate. Going forward, it adds x and z to make q.
add/up: Going backward, a gradient arrives from above: partial f, partial q, how much the graph's final output, f, moves per unit of q. Say it is two.
add/curly: Why the curly d? f depends on many inputs, so its slope in q holds all the others still: a partial derivative. In a chain with one input, like d z, d x, there is nothing to hold, and the two mean the same.
add/local: The gate multiplies it by its local slopes. For an add, both are one: nudge x or z, and q moves by the same amount.
add/copy: So an add gate passes the gradient through unchanged to both inputs: partial f, partial x and partial f, partial z each get the full two, not half of it.
mul/gate: A multiply gate works differently. Here x is three, z is minus four, and again two arrives from above.
mul/slope: q is x times z, so nudging x moves q by z times the nudge. The local slope for x is z.
mul/swap: So x gets z times the upstream gradient: minus four times two, minus eight. And z gets x times it: three times two, six.
mul/rule: Each input gets the other input's value, times the gradient from above. The multiply gate swaps.
max/gate: A max gate passes on the larger input. With x three and z five, q is five.
max/route: Nudge x a little, and q does not move at all. Nudge z, and q moves with it. So the larger input, z, gets all of the gradient, and x gets zero.
max/router: Add copies, multiply swaps, and max routes: the winner takes the whole gradient, and the other input gets nothing.
